about: The sheet for the Broad Street Station cutaway: tools/cutaway/sheet.py. Callouts are anchored to drawn parts (history ids, in the isometric view and the flat section); a badge's style is the anchored part's confidence unless `confidence` says otherwise. Callout text is a working draft, written with Claude, for the artist to edit.
title: Broad Street Station, 1943
subtitle: Cut down the middle, from the Broad Street doors to the trains
sectionCaption: The same cut, seen flat: Broad Street on the left, the trains on the right

callouts.title: Broad Street
callouts.text: The front of the station, facing West Broad Street.

callouts.title: Vestibule
callouts.text: Entrance halls on each side, with stairs and elevators up to the offices.

callouts.title: White Waiting Room
callouts.text: The main hall: a low dome over a shallow vault, with four long benches.

callouts.title: Tickets, Pullman, Information
callouts.text: Counters along the east side of the hall.

callouts.title: Colored Waiting Room
callouts.text: Virginia law kept Black and white passengers apart. This wing had its own lunch room, smoking room and toilets. The waiting rooms were segregated from the station’s opening in 1919 until January 1956, when a federal order took effect.

callouts.title: Lunch room and dining room
callouts.text: In the west wing, with the kitchen behind.

callouts.title: Baggage and parcel check
callouts.text: In the east wing, off the checking lobby.

callouts.title: The concourse
callouts.text: A long room out over the tracks.

callouts.title: Stairs
callouts.text: Down from the concourse to each platform.

callouts.title: The trains
callouts.text: RF&P and Atlantic Coast Line. 33,324 passengers on April 22, 1943, the busiest day.

callouts.title: The dome
callouts.text: Tile in 1943. The copper came in 1955.

callouts.title: Offices
callouts.text: Four floors in each wing: Trainmaster, Superintendent of Telegraph, General Superintendent.

callouts.title: Basement
callouts.text: Under the whole building, on piers. It held baggage, mail and the heating plant.

In the flat section, the departure stairs, which stand on the side lifted away, are dashed. Heights are scaled from the 1919 sections, whose figures are illegible; the first floor’s level is approximate.

page.title: Broad Street Station, 1943: the cutaway
page.summary: John Russell Pope's station cut down the middle, from the Broad Street doors to the trains, as it stood in 1943, with how sure each part is.
page.intro: Broad Street Station opened in January 1919 for the RF&P and the Atlantic Coast Line. This drawing cuts it down the middle, from the Broad Street doors through the portico, the White Waiting Room under the dome and the concourse out over the tracks, as it stood in 1943. The east half is lifted away down to its first floor, so its rooms read as a plan, and beneath it the same cut is drawn flat, with the traveler's way from the street to the train dashed in red. It belongs to the [Broad Street Station, 1943](broad-street.md) set.
page.image_alt: The cutaway sheet: the station cut down the middle above, the same cut seen flat below, and the numbered callouts beside them
page.key_intro: Every part of the drawing says how it is known, and each numbered badge shows it:
page.wayfinding_heading: Where the trains and streetcars went
page.how: The station is a model made of parts: the rooms of the first floor, the hall's octagon, its benches and counters, the portico and the concourse are traced from the first-floor plan published in The American Architect in 1919 (Plate 15), fitted by the 240-foot frontage; the levels, the dome and the basement are scaled from the sections (Plates 17 and 18), whose figures are illegible. The model is cut along one vertical plane down the station's axis. Every face the cut opens is drawn solid in ink; on the side lifted away, everything up to 1.5 m above the first floor stays, so the ground floor reads as a plan. The flat section below is the same plane seen square and level, with the building drawn 35 m deep behind it. Chris Busse drew it with isoscape, the open-source tool he built with Claude.
page.drafted: This page was drafted with Claude, Anthropic's AI (Claude Opus 5.5), and reviewed by Chris Busse. More on how we work in the [artist statement](artist-statement.md).
page.traveler_note: The small red figures are travelers drawn to scale, 1.75 m (5 ft 9 in) tall; their height is a convention, not a claim from a source. The red line is the way from the street to the train.
